opus-5.5.text:
Acute myeloid leukemia was a natural choice for us for a few reasons, some scientific and some practical.

Scientifically, AML is a cancer where the need is enormous. It's an aggressive blood cancer, outcomes for many patients, especially older adults, are still poor, and the standard of care hasn't changed dramatically in decades. At the same time, it's highly heterogeneous at the molecular level. Two patients with the same diagnosis can have very different mutations and gene expression profiles, and they respond very differently to the same drugs. That heterogeneity is exactly why combination therapy is attractive. If you can target multiple pathways at once, you have a better chance of overcoming resistance. But the number of possible drug pairs is huge, and you can't test all of them in every patient. So it's a setting where a model that predicts which combinations will be synergistic for which patients, and explains why, could make a real difference.

Practically, AML is a cancer where you can actually get the data. Because it's a blood cancer, you can obtain primary tumor cells from patients relatively easily, through blood draws or bone marrow aspirates, and you can screen those cells against many drugs and drug combinations ex vivo. We were fortunate to work with collaborators who had generated this kind of data, combining drug response measurements with molecular profiles like gene expression from the same patient samples. That's much harder to do in solid tumors, where you often have to rely on cell lines that may not reflect patient biology well.

And from a machine learning perspective, that pairing of rich molecular features with drug combination outcomes is what makes explainability meaningful. It's not enough to predict that drug A plus drug B will be synergistic. Clinicians and biologists want to know which genes or pathways are driving that prediction, so they can judge whether it makes biological sense and potentially use those features as biomarkers to select patients. In AML we could ask, for example, whether a particular differentiation state or pathway signature explains why certain combinations work. That also pushed us to make the explanations robust, because with thousands of correlated genes and relatively few samples, naive feature attributions can be unstable. Using ensembles of models to get more consistent attributions became an important part of the approach.

So AML was really the intersection of high clinical need, biological heterogeneity, and the availability of patient-derived data. That said, the framework itself isn't specific to AML. I'd love to see it applied to other cancers as similar datasets become available.

r001.rationale: The response says AML was a practical choice because patient-derived cells and paired drug-response and molecular-profile data were available.

r002.rationale: It says the framework is not specific to AML and could be applied to other cancers as similar datasets become available.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The choice of AML was actually quite deliberate, and it came from a few directions at once.

First, there's the clinical motivation. AML is a devastating disease. For older patients especially, the standard chemotherapy regimens haven't changed all that much in decades, and outcomes remain poor. So there's a real unmet need for better treatment strategies, and combination therapy is one of the most promising avenues. The idea is that if you can find pairs of drugs that work synergistically, you might get more effective treatment at lower doses with fewer side effects.

Second, and this is what made it tractable for us, AML is a blood cancer. That matters enormously from a data perspective. Getting a tumor sample from a solid cancer like pancreatic or lung cancer is invasive and difficult, so you rarely have matched molecular profiling and ex vivo drug response data for the same patient. With AML, a blood draw gives you the cancer cells directly. That meant our collaborators at Oregon Health & Science University, through the Beat AML program, could build this remarkable dataset where you have gene expression from patient samples alongside measured responses to many drugs and drug combinations on those same cells. For a machine learning approach, that's exactly the kind of paired data you need.

Third, there's a heterogeneity argument. AML is not one disease. Patients carry very different mutations, FLT3, NPM1, IDH1 and IDH2, and so on, and those differences drive very different responses to treatment. That heterogeneity is a challenge clinically, but it's also an opportunity for a model that can learn patient-specific patterns. And it's where explainability becomes essential rather than a nice-to-have. If we predict that a particular drug combination will be synergistic for a particular patient, a clinician reasonably asks why. Our approach lets us say, this prediction is driven by the expression of these genes, which point to this biological pathway, and that gives a hypothesis you can actually check against known biology.

So I'd put it this way. We didn't pick AML because it's easy. We picked it because it sits at the intersection of high clinical need, unusually rich data, and biological complexity that genuinely rewards an interpretable approach. The methods themselves aren't specific to AML, and our hope is to extend them to other cancers as comparable data becomes available. But AML was the right place to prove that the combination of prediction and explanation could produce something a biologist or clinician would trust and act on.

r001.rationale: The response says AML was tractable because blood samples enabled a rich dataset pairing gene expression with drug-response measurements, supporting the approach.

r002.rationale: It says the methods are not specific to AML and could extend to other cancers as comparable data becomes available.

astra-6.text: I view acute myeloid leukemia as a starting point, rather than a limitation of the approach. It’s a setting where identifying effective drug combinations is an important clinical problem, and where we can ask whether the model’s explanations point to meaningful biology. We want to understand not just which combinations might work, but why they might work and how that could vary across patients. The broader goal is to develop an approach that can be applied to other cancers, provided we have the appropriate data and experimental validation.

r001.rationale: It says AML is a setting for studying drug combinations, but does not identify data availability as the reason it was chosen.

r002.rationale: It says the approach can be applied to other cancers, given appropriate data and experimental validation.

sol-6.1.text:
Acute myeloid leukemia is a compelling setting because there’s a real need for better treatments, and the disease is very heterogeneous. Different patients can respond quite differently to the same drugs. So the question is not just whether a combination works, but why it works and for which patients.

From a research perspective, it also gives us a setting where we can connect molecular measurements with drug responses. With an explainable AI approach, we want to use that connection to identify potential synergistic combinations and generate hypotheses about the biological mechanisms behind them. AML is a starting point for that approach; the broader goal is to make it useful across other cancers as well.

r001.rationale: The response mentions connecting molecular measurements with drug responses, but does not say data availability was the reason AML was chosen.

r002.rationale: It says AML is a starting point and the approach’s broader goal is to be useful across other cancers.
